title: How did Bonnie and Clyde (1967) usher in “New Hollywood”?

commenti.body:
A wave is never truly started by one movie, its started by a string of movies, of which Bonnie and Clyde was obviously one. 

And yes, nudity and violence were on the up even within more traditional Hollywood movies at the time. Still, it was Bonnie and Clyde and films like it that brought the thing to a boiling point. Sure, its not a super graphic film, but the atmosphere is far more depraved than anything you'd see in a Hollywood film up to that time.

>A really consistent view I see is that Bonnie And Clyde single-handedly kicked off the 70s New Hollywood movement (auteur directors, graphic sex and violence, moving away from the studio system etc etc).

I don't think this is the argument anyone makes, at least not any serious film historian or critic. It's a complex historical issue that goes way beyond just one film. For one, you need to understand the Hays code and specifically how its grip over the industry weakened in the 60s until it was eventually replaced by the MPAA. The Hays code is something you could (and people have) written entire books about, but the short version is that it was a sell imposed censorship standard Hollywood abided by to avoid government censorship. Some of the core aspects of it were limited depictions of graphic violence, little to no depictions or even mentions of sex or nudity, no illicit drug use, criminal behavior always had to be depicted negatively and the perpetrators punished in some way. 

Artists skirted and subverted the Hays code in all sorts of ways, but the late 60s saw a real sea change in Hollywood since it actually became possible to depict graphic violence and films didn't have to have the conservative morality that was often enforced previously. Bonnie and Clyde is held up because it's one of the earliest examples of these changes being seen en masse in a single film but it didn't single handedly kick off the New Hollywood era.

>auteur directors

Auteur theory is probably the most broadly misunderstood concepts in film theory and criticism. The idea was developed by French directors/critics like Jean Luc Godard and Francois Truffaut, and Truffaut himself coined the term in *1954* in an article in Cahiers du Cinema. It's very important to understand that the concept was developed *around* films made in the Hollywood studio system and the Hays code by directors with strong authorial voices like Howard Hawks, Nicholas Ray, and Alfred Hitchcock amongst others. It was not something that sprung up out of nowhere in the late 60s and 70s and the auteur directors of America of that era like Scorsese or Coppola were equally influenced by Cahiers du Cinema as the older generation of American directors.

You have to remember that Faye Dunaway was a revelation. Everyone was looking for the next Bette Davis, the next Joan Crawford. A beautiful woman with the acting chops. Times had changed towards more verism in acting, and Faye was lightning in a bottle. Audiences were intrigued by realism. Joan was a gorgeous actress, but you always saw the structure surrounding her performances… not affected, not mannered… it’s just a style. Faye burst onto the scene but what set her apart was that she looked like a supermodel and she could act in the new style. People watched Bonnie and Clyde and wanted this new style. Later Faye would later have her career destroyed. But for a time she was a catalyst for the new movement.

Yes.

And I think in general it's important to remember that 'waves' and 'movements' are, for the most part, abstractions, identified in hindsight by scholars and critics. Wordsworth and Coleridge did not call themselves "Romantic poets" and their contemporary William Blake was simply too in his own world to be part of any movement; Picasso and Braque did not call themselves "cubists," Satyajit Ray is often identified as part of Parallel cinema but if you read his writing you'll quickly learn that he was just doing his own thing as a regional Bengali filmmaker, not really involved in some wider movement.

I’m interested to see the replies here! I recently thrifted an interesting 1972 book, [It’s Only a Movie](https://eric.ed.gov/?q=movies+AND+effect+AND+people&pg=2&id=ED074703), that holds Bonnie and Clyde up as the pinnacle of film-making at the time.

Really?

How do you think it compares to *Badlands*?

“Pinnacle” is maybe a strong word, since it features so many different opinions. Bonnie and Clyde definitely haunt the book - the movie comes up shockingly often.  

It’s been years since I’ve seen either movie, but iirc they have a similar vibe! They both made being on the run very sexy and very cool.

And, of course, *Bonnie and Clyde* in particular is kind of an unofficial remake of *Gun Crazy* (1950). 

Per that book, what were the really canonical films as of the early seventies?

From me it’s “In Cold Blood (1967)” by Richard Brooks. That film had some of the most stunning visuals and creative storytelling during that time period. Funny thing is it’s rarely ever mentioned. I mean the editing, cinematography, score, and direction feels like nothing else during that period. 

That moment when it’s raining outside Perry’s cell and the raindrops look like tears on Perry’s face as he talks about his dad. Man why don’t people talk about this film? Everything about it screams “New Hollywood”

I took [a few pictures](https://imgur.com/a/m7JKvDR) of my favorite pages + most of the Bonnie & Clyde content.  

Hitchcock comes up over and over again, of course. Orson Welles. Andy Warhol and Picasso, because the book also loves art and celebrity of all forms. Mae West gets her due, as does The Jazz Singer. Fellini, John Ford, Bruce Connor, Bergman, and Truffaut frequently invoked. Rosemary’s Baby, Casablanca, The African Queen, and The Graduate are favorites.  

It seems to be an exercise book for film lovers and students, so it has references galore lol.

Interesting how much Truffaut's reputation has taken a hit in the last 50 years. 

Also thinking about how Arthur Penn never really became a canonical director, despite both *Bonnie and Clyde* and *Little Big Man*, two key New Hollywood films.

New Hollywood is kind of a fake movement. It's just a reaction to the times than a proper view on cinema. Studios wanted to refresh the product. Bonnie and Clyde is clearly a product that looks at a young demographic with new faces and a general new look.

There's a perfect storm of things that happen:

 - In 1957, the US Supreme rules that the governments can ban material that is "utterly without redeeming social value":

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roth_v._United_States

 - In 1963, Eric Jonhston (the MPAA's president) dies. He is replaced with Jack Valenti in 1966. Valenti pushes Hollywood to adopt something like the modern rating system, which is fully adopted in 1968:

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hays_Code#Abandonment

 - In 1967, negotiations between Francois Truffant and WB break down. Beatty buys the rights to make David Newman and Robert Benton's script. He fails to secure a director and makes it himself for $2.5 million ($25 million in 2023 $$$):

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bonnie_and_Clyde_(film)#Production_and_style

It goes on to gross $70 million ($700 million in 2023 $$$).

Over the next 10 years a string of other young creatives who are informed by a wide array of influences secure financing to make small, weird movies that defy convention and find huge audiences.
